chunks: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ṣafwān, from al-ʿAlāʾ, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said:
"The menstrual interval does not occur in less than ten [days]; whatever exceeds that, the least it can be is ten, from the time she becomes pure until she sees blood."
Al-Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, said: Whenever a woman sees blood for less than three days, that is not hayd, and she must make up what she left of the salat.

What has preceded indicates this, namely that when it is established that the minimum days of hayd are three days and its maximum is ten days, it is established that whatever is less than three and exceeds ten is not from it. And if it is not from hayd, then there is no disagreement among the Muslims that salat and sawm are obligatory upon her, and she must make up the salat; and this is further supported by that.

key_terms.الدَّمَ: the blood whose legal status is being assessed
key_terms.الصَّلَاةِ: salat (prayer), which remains obligatory when the blood is not hayd
key_terms.الصَّوْمُ: sawm (fasting), which remains obligatory when the blood is not hayd
key_terms.الْقُرْءُ: the menstrual interval or cycle discussed in the ruling
key_terms.عَشَرَةٍ: ten days, the minimum interval of purity and the maximum duration mentioned
key_terms.قَضَاءُ: making up an omitted act of worship

ai.seo_question: What is the minimum and maximum duration of hayd, and what is the ruling if blood is seen for less than three days?
ai.summary: This text sets out a legal ruling regarding hayd: its minimum duration is three days and its maximum is ten days, and the interval of purity between occurrences cannot be less than ten days. Therefore, blood seen for less than three days is not treated as hayd, and the woman remains obligated to perform salat and sawm, with missed salat requiring qaḍāʾ.
